entries.title: 1. Use Nulb as the Staging Ground
entries.body:
The most logical path to the Temple is from the village of Nulb, located just a half-day’s journey (six miles) east of Hommlet. 

The DM can emphasize that while Nulb is a "scurvy place" of pirates and smugglers, it serves as the gateway to the "fountainhead of wickedness" hidden in the hills nearby.

entries.title: 2. Describe the Sensory "Aura of Evil"
entries.body: As players approach, the DM should utilize the environmental descriptions found in the sources to build dread. The vegetation becomes twisted and unnaturally colored, with thorns that clutch and weeds that emit a foul stench. The DM should mention the pervading fear that hangs over the area like a tangibly thick cloud, causing sounds to seem muffled or unnaturally grating.

entries.title: 3. Leverage "Old-Timer" Clues
entries.body: If players are hesitant, the DM can have them consult old-timers in Hommlet or members of the Town Council. These NPCs can relate the "Secret History of the Temple," explaining that while the upper works were destroyed a decade ago, the great doors were merely sealed with mighty wards to bind the evil within. This establishes the Temple as a place of both great peril and "treasures secreted deep underground".

entries.title: 4. Introduce Nefarious "Guides"
entries.body: The DM can use Temple spies to lure the players to the ruins. For example, Zert (Area I 6) or the traders Rannos Davl and Gremag (Area 13) may pretend to be interested in monster slaying while actually leading the party into an ambush or reporting their progress to Temple authorities. These agents might "insinuate themselves" into the party to lead them directly to the Temple's gates.

entries.title: 5. Provide the Visual Goal
entries.body: Finally, the DM should describe the physical remains of the Upper Works. As the players emerge from the "Overgrown Track," they will see dark mounds of gray rubble, the "leprous gray" Temple itself, and the jagged stub of a large tower (the Broken Tower) jutting from the northeast corner of the shattered wall. Seeing the massive bronze doors sealed with iron and bearing silvery-glowing runes serves as the final physical orientation toward the dungeon entry.

entries.title: 1. Learn About Bandits
entries.body:
Ostler Gundigoot announces during the session that his supplies have not arrived, because of bandits. 

Other members of the village will have similar complaints.

entries.title: 2. Extraordinary Council Meeting
entries.body: The Council will call a meeting to hear the village's concerns about the enroaching bandit problem.

entries.title: F. Glovers' Gate
entries.body:
You cross town through lanes thick with dusk, past the canal's slow gurgle, until Glovers' Gate looms ahead. Its arch sags under old weight, iron gates propped half-open by stone wedges, hinges pitted and silent. Dust drifts through from the plain beyond, catching in cracks where mortar has long crumbled.

The Merchants' Ward unfolds beyond, a maze of stone houses built tall by hands that once dreamed big. Facades bear faded carvings—ships with full sails, scales heaped with gold—now worn smooth by rain and neglect. Windows gape dark, glass cracked or gone, shutters hanging crooked like broken fingers. Vines choke cornices, their leaves dry and brittle.

At the ward's heart squats the Stock Exchange, a broad hall of gray slabs, its columns thick but leaning, steps hollowed deep by boots that no longer rush. Inside, echoes chase voices grown hoarse with haggling; ledgers slump on dusty tables, ink faded to ghosts. Braziers smolder low, casting long shadows over men in threadbare velvet, their eyes sharp but shoulders bowed. The air tastes of cold metal and parchment rot. No banners fly. The wind whines through empty market frames, stirring papers no one bothers to claim.

entries.title: A. Main Gate
entries.body:
You step through Ostwerk's main gate, and the square hits like a gust—raw voices, the slap of bare feet on stone, the creak of cart wheels biting into grooves. Tall houses crowd in, their walls stained with old rain, shutters half-open to spill yellow lamplight onto the cobbles below.

Merchants squat by low stalls, scales clinking as they weigh salt and dried fish. Bread steams from clay ovens, its crust split and golden; river mud clings to baskets of pale roots hauled from the canal. Smoke hangs low from braziers, threading with the tang of wet wool and iron.

Children weave through legs, chasing a rag ball that bounces off barrels, their shouts sharp and fleeting. At the fountain's cracked basin, moss veils the stone fish that spits a thin stream—travelers cup their hands there, murmuring over chipped mugs while water patters into the green pool.

A canal gleams alongside the nearest lane, its surface rippling with laundry poles thrust deep in the muck; slow bubbles rise from unseen depths. Porters grunt under crates that drip sawdust. A fiddler draws bow across gut strings, notes thin and wandering. Hammer strikes ring from two streets over, steady as a pulse, drowned now by the crowd's low roar. Laundry snaps overhead in the breeze, faded rags twisting like signals no one reads.

entries.title: B. Palantine Plaza
entries.body:
The lane climbs from the square, away from the canal's murmur, past shuttered warehouses that smell of damp grain and tar. Stone underfoot turns rougher, steps worn into the slope by boots that hurry both ways.

At the crest sits the citadel, a squat block of weathered granite, its walls low and thick but cracked where ivy claws in. Banners droop from rusted poles—faded sable on yellow, edges frayed. Narrow windows glow with tallow light; shadows shift behind iron bars.

Barracks huddle to one side, a row of timber sheds with sagging roofs, doors ajar to spill sour ale fumes and the rasp of whetstones on blade. Guards slouch in doorways, mail glinting dull, hands loose on hilts or coins. Laughter barks out, low and shared, as a merchant's cart rolls past unchallenged.

Higher still, the count's house looms—a tall, narrow keep with a single turret, its timbers black with pitch, roof tiles missing in patches. Windows are small, draped in heavy cloth; smoke leaks slow from a lone chimney. Servants scurry at the gate, eyes down, while voices murmur inside—sharp, pleading tones cut short by the wind.

No trumpets sound here. The air hangs heavy with oil lamps and unwashed leather. Footsteps echo too loud on the empty cobbles; eyes watch from slits, but none step forth.

entries.title: Mirkmire
entries.body:
Mist coils low through Mirkmire, threading black water and twisted roots that snag at boots. Overgrown swamp bleeds into woodland, alders leaning drunken over pools where lily pads rot yellow, their edges curling like old parchment.

Ancient mounds hunch amid the tangle—low domes of packed earth, fringed with moss and bramble, sunk half into mire. Stone slabs jut from summits, carved faces worn to blanks, mouths agape as if frozen mid-shout. Vines choke the bases, thick as ropes, dripping slow with sap and rain.

The air chokes on peat rot and stagnant bloom, undercut by faint iron tang from submerged iron. Willows weep into fog, branches scraping like nails on wood. No birds call; only bubbles break the surface, lazy from unseen depths, and the hush of leaves in a breeze that carries no warmth.

entries.title: Nedunaim
entries.body:
The road from the Kron Hills spills onto Neduniam's windy plain, a vast sweep of yellow grass bowing flat under gusts that howl from the foothills. Scrub and thistle clump the earth, roots clawing shallow into chalky soil cracked by old drought.

Fifteen years back, steel clashed here—ranks broken on rises still scarred with mass graves, their mounds settled low, turf torn by burrowing foxes. Rusted spearheads glint half-buried after rains, tangled in bleached bones that surface like pale roots. A lone stele tilts at the field's heart, its inscription pitted blank, surrounded by rings of fire-blackened stone where campfires once roared.

Wind shrieks constant, whipping dust into veils that sting the eyes and carry faint rot from churned earth. Ravens wheel overhead, dropping feathers that spin away unanswered. No banners mark the spot; only grass whispers over steel, and shadows of clouds race like routed cavalry.

entries.title: Dyvers
entries.body:
Dyvers is a great walled city located many days' travel to the east of Hommlet. It is strategically situated on the shores of the Lake of Unknown Depths, also known as the Nyr Dyv.

The journey from Hommlet to Dyvers typically takes travelers through the village of Sobanwych, which sits approximately halfway along the route.
   
The city is a major destination for the flow of the Velverdyva River, which moves eastward past Verbobonc and Nulb before emptying into the Nyr Dyv at Dyvers.
   
Within the region's history, one faction claims that the Evil that eventually plagued Hommlet originally migrated west from Dyvers, though others dispute this, asserting it crept up from the Wild Coast.

As a major urban center, it is the home of wealthy merchants who travel the Lowroad. For example, merchants rescued from the Moathouse dungeons often hail from Dyvers and promise to send rewards back to their rescuers once they reach the safety of their homes there.

Because of its size and distance from the Temple ruins, it is seen as a place where those fleeing the law or rival factions—such as defeated brigand leaders—might go to seek "better things" or a fresh start.

entries.title: Verbobonc
entries.body:
Verbobonc is a major city of 11,600 inhabitants and serves as the capital of the Viscounty of Verbobonc, which has a total regional population of approximately 35,000. It is situated roughly 30 leagues (90 miles) northwest of the village of Hommlet. The city is strategically located along the south bank of the Velverdyva River, a massive waterway that connects various great realms and serves as a primary route for trade and travel.

As a significant urban center, Verbobonc offers a greater scope of information and superior equipment than can be found in smaller outposts like Hommlet or Nulb. The city features several prominent landmarks and administrative buildings, including the palace of Viscount Wilfrick, the Mayor's residence, City Hall, and numerous Guild halls. 

Reflecting the political alliances of the region, the city also contains strongholds for the local gnomes and elves.

Politically and militarily, Verbobonc is a vital ally to the forces of Good; the Viscount of Verbobonc, in conjunction with the Archcleric of Veluna, is financing the construction of the new castle and guard tower in Hommlet to secure the region against a resurgence of evil. Materials for this project are frequently transported from Verbobonc via heavily laden wagon caravans. However, the city is not entirely safe, as it has been infiltrated by spies of the Temple of Elemental Evil who keep a close watch on any adventurers who appear to be tracking the source of the region's corruption.

entries.title: Sobanwych
entries.body:
Sobanwych is a village located in the central part of the Flanaess. 

It serves as a midpoint on the long journey from the village of Hommlet to the great walled city of Dyvers, which sits many days' travel to the east on the shores of the Lake of Unknown Depths (Nyr Dyv). 

Travelers following the route from Hommlet toward the Nyr Dyv will find Sobanwych situated approximately halfway along the route.

entries.title: The Gnarly Wood
entries.body:
The Gnarley Wood (also referred to as the Gnarley Forest) is a vast wilderness area located southeast and east of the village of Hommlet. It encompasses miles and miles of forest stretching toward the Wild Coast, Woolly Bay, and the Sea of Gearnat.

The forest is geographically connected to the region's major waterways, as the Velverdyva River flows through the Gnarley on its eastward path toward the Lake of Unknown Depths (Nyr Dyv).

Politically and religiously, the wood is a center of power for the Old Faith. Jaroo Ashstaff, the Druid of the Grove in Hommlet, is actually an agent of the druids of Gnarley Wood. He was dispatched from the forest to the Hommlet region specifically to monitor the Ruins of the Moathouse and the Temple of Elemental Evil, ensuring that the defeated cult does not rise again to threaten the surrounding realms.

entries.title: The Kron Hills
entries.body:
South from Hommlet, the road climbs into the Kron Hills—ancient ridges folded like old parchment, their crests tufted with scrub pine and gorse. Gray stone outcrops jut from slopes worn smooth by wind and rain, hollows pooling shadow even at noon.

The path forks under a weathered cairn, one branch snaking southeast through grassy vales toward Ostverk's dust, then onward to Celene's golden haze. Westward, it burrows deeper into gnomish highlands, past Greenway Valley's patchwork fields, where water wheels creak and woodsmoke threads the air.

Gnome steadings dot the hills—burrows faced with round doors of hammered copper, green with patina, half-sunk into earth banks bright with thrift flowers. Chimney pipes belch peat haze; the tang of forge embers and baked clay hangs sharp. Picks ring faint from tunnel mouths, joined by the yip of terriers and low laughter like stones in a tumbler.

Caves gape here and there, their lips fringed with moss, floors crunching with old bone and rusted mail. Ruins crown higher tors—crumbled walls of cyclopean stone, slabs split by root and frost, wind moaning through gaps where once beams groaned. No dragon's stink lingers; its bones bleach somewhere unseen, picked clean by ravens three years gone.

The hills breathe watchful quiet, a buffer of earth and craft between realms, their folk's eyes keen from hidden slits. Footfalls echo too clear on deer paths; somewhere, a gemcutter's rasp pauses, then resumes.

entries.title: Veluna
entries.body:
Far to the West of Hommlet, the land softens into Veluna's realm, where Silver Elves weave their quiet dominion between ancient boles. East of the Lortmil Mountains' jagged teeth, the forest of Vestarlynor waits—its canopy a silver-green haze, leaves shimmering like chainmail in the slanted light.

Needle-thin trunks rise straight and tall, bark pale as moonlight, etched with faint runes that pulse once when you pass. Moss clings in velvet cushions to roots that twist above ground like exposed veins. The air hums, thick with the scent of crushed ferns and sap, undercut by a chill that raises hairs on the neck.

Deeper in, the court's glades open. Throneroot arches form natural halls, woven with living vines that bear glowing silver nuts. Elves move silent as shadows, their cloaks rippling like quicksilver, eyes catching light in twin glints. A brook chuckles over crystal pebbles, its water cold and tasting of minerals. No underbrush snarls the paths; silence presses close, broken only by the distant snap of a twig or the sigh of wind through high branches.

entries.title: Celene
entries.body:
Southward, the trail dips into Celene's valley, cradled by mountains whose peaks burn gold at dawn. The Golden Elves' realm unfurls here, locked in eternal autumn—leaves drift in slow spirals from boughs heavy with amber and crimson, carpeting the earth in crackling layers that release a scent of dry earth and faint decay.

Tall oaks stand sentinel, their trunks girt with golden bark that peels in thin curls, branches woven into graceful arches. Mist clings low in the hollows, veiling roots that gleam wet from hidden springs. The air bites crisp, spiced with fallen mast and woodsmoke from unseen hearths.

At the valley's heart rises the Stately House, a spire of living wood gilded by moss and lichen, its balconies hung with tapestries of woven leaves that rustle without wind. Elves glide beneath, their skin warm-toned, hair like spun copper catching the slant light. Faint harp notes thread the stillness, chased by the rustle of leaves underfoot. Shadows lengthen early here; the sun hangs low, painting all in hues of burnished metal.

entries.title: Khudzul Gal
entries.body:
The distant home of the Dwarrow folk, or "Dwarves", Khudzul Gal is more gestured towards, rather than at any one place, on most maps. 

This is because for those who dwell within the southlands, and of teh houses of Celene and Veluna, little is known about the lands beyond the Velvydyr River.
